This is game 10 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll continue at 20k, review the recent games, and focus on securing two viable bases and counting area early. I’ll play to completion and save the full record and concrete lessons for game 11.

# Game 9: Black vs 20k — W+42

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 67–68: 66 stone moves and two passes.
Final captures: Black 4, White 16. A ko occurred at A1 after move 50; no invalid move occurred.

20k was retained deliberately. This is the fifth loss at 20k; no successful rank is established.

## Records and verified score
- game-009.sgf contains all 68 moves.
- game-009-log.json contains all 34 play responses, every returned board and reconstructed current-board group/liberty inventory, complete moves, opponent-selection metadata and final area.
- Official result: White wins by 42.
- Independent final-board count: Black 17 stones + 6 territory = 23; White 29 stones + 29 territory = 58. With komi, White scores 65 against 23. No neutral points or dead-stone removals were needed.
- Black territory consists of three separate two-point spaces: J1/J2, H4/J4 and J6/J7.
- White captured fifteen connected left-side Black stones at move 52, in addition to the isolated A1 stone at move 50.

## Opening: two sides, neither initially proven alive
1 B C3, 2 W F6, 3 B C7, 4 W D7,
5 B C6, 6 W D6, 7 B D5, 8 W E5,
9 B C5, 10 W D4, 11 B G3, 12 W D3,
13 B C4, 14 W E2, 15 B G5, 16 W G6.

C5 connected D5 to the upper-left chain; C4 joined that chain to C3. G3 was played at move 11 to establish a second foothold before White occupied the whole right side. This changed the opening from games 5 and 7, but did not produce a win or validate the individual moves.

17 B H6, 18 W F4, 19 B G4 connected G3/G5.
20 W C8, 21 B B7, 22 W B8 reduced the top of the left region.
23 B H7, 24 W G2, 25 B H2, 26 W F2, 27 B H3 connected the lower-right stones while blocking White's immediate H2 continuation.
28 W C2, 29 B B2, 30 W B1, 31 B B3 connected the left-side lower extension, but White B1 denied a connected Black first-line boundary.

32 W A7, 33 B A6, 34 W A8, 35 B B6 connected the left edge stone safely.
36 W G7, 37 B G8, 38 W F8, 39 B H8 connected the upper-right extension immediately. Unlike game 7's F9 stone, G8 was not left disconnected during another fight.

The early estimate treated whole left and right columns as potential. That was too generous to guide a decision: there were no verified two-eyed groups, and White could undercut both ends. The group inventory ran, but it did not turn the shrinking eye space into an early correction.

A retrospective geometric outline after move 35 gives only 18 left points: the eleven Black stones plus A1/A2/A3/A4/A5/B4/B5. A1 was already adjacent to White B1, and A4 was an invasion point. These were unsecured points, not territory. The eventual right side scored 23. Even adding an unchanged eighteen-point left outline to that final right side would total only 41, below Black's 45-point winning target. This comparison is an area warning, not a claim that the left outline could all be saved.

## Main failure: the left eye space became one eye plus a losing ko
40 W A4 invaded the left eye space.
41 B B4 blocked its inward extension.
42 W A5 left White A4/A5 with A3/B5 as liberties, while the twelve-stone Black group had A2/A3/B5.
43 B B5 reduced White to A3, but also reduced Black to A2/A3.
44 W A2 put the thirteen-stone Black group in atari at A3. White A4/A5 also had only A3.

45 B A3 captured A4/A5. Rebuilding the board showed the fourteen-stone Black group had only A4/A5: a single two-point eye space. The capture did not establish life.
46 W C1 connected White B1 to C2.
White could already have killed the actual move-45 group with W A4, B A5 capturing one, W A4 capturing fifteen. This is a short manually read variation, not a played sequence. In that position White A2 was still present and supplied no Black liberty.

Actual continuation:
47 B A1 captured isolated White A2 and temporarily opened A2 for the main group. The new Black A1 stone itself had only A2.
48 W A4 entered the two-point eye; Black now had A2/A5.
49 B A5 captured A4, creating a true eye at A4, but A2 remained dependent on isolated Black A1.
50 W A2 captured Black A1. The tool marked A1 as ko. Black's fifteen-stone left group had only A4.

Black could not recapture A1 immediately. Connecting at A2 before move 50 would also not have solved the eye problem: after move 48, B A2 would leave the combined group only A5, where White could capture it.

There was no demonstrated forcing ko threat worth fifteen stones. 51 B H5 instead connected the upper and lower right groups; White ignored it and 52 W A4 captured all fifteen left stones. This was a real ko for life, not unconditional life and not seki. H5 was a consolidation move, not a forcing ko threat.

The correction belongs before the first-line undercut and A4 invasion. Reconsider left-side development around moves 29–35, and name a complete pair of secured eye spaces before spending moves on G8/H8. No single replacement has been verified to save the left group or win. B4 alone is not a demonstrated cure: it was played in the actual fight and the group still died.

## What survived: connected boundaries around separate eye spaces
51 B H5 joined G5 to H6/H7/H8/G8.
53 B H1 preserved the lower corner boundary; 54 W G1 did not remove it.
55 B J3 connected to H3 and closed the upper end of J1/J2.
57 B J5 connected to H5 and separated H4/J4 from the upper edge.

After move 57:
- J1/J2 was one two-point eye space, bordered by connected Black H1/H2/J3.
- H4/J4 was a separate two-point eye space, bordered by connected Black G4/H3/H5/J3/J5.
Thus the main group already had two independent eyes. H1 alone had not proved life; the dividing boundary stones J3/J5 mattered.

White G9/H9 reduced the upper boundary. 59 B J8 connected to H8 and stopped further descent along the edge. 60 W F9 linked the top invaders to F8, and 62 W J9 took the remaining corner point.
61 B F5, 63 B F3, 65 B E3 claimed three central boundary points. White E4 at move 64 connected F4 to the central White group.
The final J6/J7 space was a third independent two-point eye, bounded by H6/H7/J5/J8.

67 B pass, 68 W pass accepted the losing score. The surviving right group had 23 area; obtaining life did not repair the deficit.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k. Five losses provide no successful rank; 9d remains the long-term target.
2. Treat the first-line undercut as an eye-boundary emergency, not merely a loss of a few points. B2/B3 connectivity did not replace the missing Black B1 boundary.
3. After capturing eye-space invaders, count the resulting independent eyes. Capturing A4/A5 gave one two-point eye; capturing A2 then introduced a ko dependency through isolated A1.
4. A ko for a large group's life needs real threats. H5 was valuable consolidation, but White could ignore it and capture fifteen.
5. Make the area count concrete while groups still have choices. The left outline was both small and unsettled; an optimistic count of whole columns obscured this.
6. Preserve the demonstrated right-side boundaries. H1/J3/J5 secured two independent eye spaces, and J8 contained the top reduction. Their success does not validate the whole opening or establish a winning pattern in other positions.

All choices and tactical variations were manual. Code recorded responses, parsed present-board groups and liberties, converted the moves to SGF and counted final present-board area. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or program selecting/ranking/recommending moves was used.

# Game 8: White vs 20k — B+8

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 75–76. There were 76 moves: 71 stone moves and five passes (58, 63, 71, 75, 76).
Final captures: Black 11, White 4. No ko or invalid move occurred.

20k was retained deliberately. This is the fourth loss at 20k; no successful rank is established. The smaller margin does not by itself prove stronger play or validate the opening.

## Records and verified score
- game-008.sgf contains all 76 moves.
- game-008-log.json contains opponent selection, every returned position, present-board group/liberty inspections, complete moves and final area.
- Official result: Black wins by 8 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 31 stones + 17 territory = 48; White 25 stones + 8 territory = 33. White plus komi = 40. No neutral points or dead-stone removals were needed.
- White territory: A9, B8, A7, D7, E9, G8, H9, J8.
- White's region was all 27 points in rows 7–9 plus A6–F6: 33 points. Black owned the other 48.
- At that split, shifting four points from Black to White draws; five wins. This is area arithmetic, not evidence of an available five-point move.

## Opening: three corner approaches were not three living groups
1 B E5, 2 W C7, 3 B G3, 4 W C3, 5 B C5,
6 W G7, 7 B G5, 8 W E7, 9 B E3,
10 W C6, 11 B H6, 12 W H7, 13 B J6,
14 W D6, 15 B F7, 16 W F6, 17 B G6,
18 W F8, 19 B F5, 20 W E6, 21 B D5.

The opening built a surviving top wall. Black F7 had only F8/F6; White F6 put it in atari, Black G6 ignored that atari, and White F8 captured it. E6 then connected C6/D6/E7/F6. This is a concrete opponent mistake, not proof that the opening forces a capture.

The early count was explicitly provisional: about 27 top points plus 9–12 lower-left points. The corner's life was not established. The top ultimately grew to 33, but the lower-left contributed zero. Counting its potential correctly as unsecured was useful; failing to secure it still lost the game.

White C3 was left alone from move 4 until move 22, while Black took C5/E3 and completed the central D5 boundary. Earlier lower-left development, such as reconsidering B3 or C2 around move 10 instead of continuing the top, remains an unverified candidate. C2 alone is not a life pattern; game 6 already demonstrated that the left eye boundary and the dividing move also matter.

## Lower-left: two routes closed, then E4 added no liberties
22 W C4, 23 B B5, 24 W D4, 25 B B4,
26 W B3, 27 B D2, 28 W C2, 29 B D1,
30 W C1, 31 B A3.

After Black A3, White C4/D4/C3/B3/C2/C1 had only E4, D3, B2 and B1. C1 stopped the right first-line undercut, but A3 removed the left boundary needed for a corner eye space. No pair of eyes existed.

32 W D3, 33 B E2 connected Black E3 to D2/D1.
White's seven-stone group then had only E4/B2/B1.
34 W E4, 35 B F4 left the eight-stone group only B2/B1.
E4 extended into a closed strip: it added F4 as a liberty, which Black immediately occupied. It neither escaped nor established an eye.

The corner extensions did not save this actual position:
- After move 35, W B2, B A2 leaves the enlarged White group only B1; W B1 leaves it only A1; B A1 captures it. Black's A2 connects to A3.
- Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves White only A1; W A1 is legal and extends to A2 as its sole liberty. B A2 then connects B2 to A3 and captures all ten White stones. A1 is not suicide in this variation: A2 is initially empty.

These are manual variations, not played moves or program search. They show why two remaining corner liberties were insufficient here.

Actual cleanup:
43 B A2, 45 B B1 put White in atari at B2;
47 B B2 captured all eight lower-left stones.
White did not add further doomed extensions.

The strategic correction belongs before A3/E2/F4 close the base and escape. No single earlier replacement has been verified to save the group or win.

## Right invasion: a narrow edge strip, not a base
36 W H3, 37 B H4, 38 W H2, 39 B G2,
40 W H1, 41 B G1.

After G1, White H3/H2/H1 had exactly J3/J2/J1 as liberties. All were in one straight edge strip. H4 and G3/G2/G1 barred the outside; J4 was not a secured White boundary. H1 preserved the corner approach but did not make two eyes.

53 B J3, 55 B J2 left the group only J1.
White J1 was suicide: Black J2/J3 retained J4 as a liberty.
57 B J1 captured all three White stones.

The invasion had no verified life plan when played. This repeats the earlier mistake of counting available edge points without their boundaries and timing. The lower region was already constrained; entering it late did not replace the lost corner.

## What survived: explicit eyes and successful invasion defense
42 W F7 joined F8, E7/F6 and G7/H7.
44 W B6 and 46 W A6 secured the left end of the wall.
48 W J7 closed the right edge; 49 B A5 fixed the left boundary.
50 W E8, 52 W D8, 54 W D9, 56 W F9 established:
- D7, bounded by connected White C7/D6/E7/D8.
- E9, bounded by connected White D9/E8/F9.
The main group had two independent true eyes before the later top invasions.

58 W pass, 59 B A7, 60 W B7, 61 B B8,
62 W C8, 63 B pass, 64 W C9, 65 B E1,
66 W A8 captured A7; 67 B C1;
68 W B9 captured B8.
C8/C9 secured the boundary before the captures. A8 retained A7/A9 immediately after capturing A7; no counter-capture freed the invaders. It later had A7/A9/B8, all bordered elsewhere by the living main group.

69 B H9, 70 W H8, 71 B pass,
72 W G9, 73 B J4, 74 W J9 captured H9.
The isolated J9 stone had H9/J8 afterward; both points were also adjacent to the living main group. Neither immediate Black entry could capture it. White's final A8 and J9 were separate stones supported by that living surrounding group, not standalone groups with two eyes.

75 B pass, 76 W pass finished the game.
The invasion defenses preserved 33 area; they did not repair the deficit.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k. Four losses still provide no successful level.
2. A three-corner opening is only potential. Prioritize a second living base before repeatedly enlarging a top group that already has ample eye room.
3. Reassess the lower-left before the side undercut. C1 alone did not preserve the base; Black A3 invalidated its left eye boundary.
4. Identify the destination of an escape before extending. E4 added one temporary liberty F4, which Black filled immediately.
5. Three empty edge points need secured boundaries and a dividing move. H3/H2/H1 with only J1/J2/J3 was not alive.
6. The top defense worked because the main group already had D7/E9 and the invading stones' capture liberties were checked. Preserve this concrete reading, while separating life from a sufficient area count.

All choices and tactical variations were manual. Code inspected only returned current boards, counted groups/liberties and final area, recorded responses and converted the move record to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 6: White vs 20k — B+24

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 81–82. There were 82 moves: 79 stone moves and three passes (72, 81, 82). The displayed next-move number was 83.
Final captures: Black 18, White 6. No ko or invalid move occurred.

20k was retained deliberately to practise living groups and measurable results. This second loss at 20k leaves no successful rank established; 9d remains the target.

## Records and score
- game-006.sgf: complete 82-move record.
- game-006-log.json: opponent selection, every returned position, complete moves, final groups and independent final-area inspection.
- Official result: Black wins by 24 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 56, White 25, no neutral points. White's 7 komi gives 32 against 56.
- White finished with one living 21-stone upper group and four territory points: B9, E9, H8 and H9.
- Black had 34 stones and 22 territory points. Both failed White groups were actually captured, so no manual removal of dead stones was needed for this count.

## Main correction: the lower-left was NOT seki
Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D4, 4 W C4, 5 B D3,
6 W G7, 7 B C5, 8 W C2, 9 B D2,
10 W B4, 11 B B5, 12 W A4, 13 B B2,
14 W B3, 15 B A5, 16 W C1, 17 B A2,
18 W B1, 19 B D1.

After move 19:
- White A4/B1/B3/B4/C1/C2/C3/C4 had only A1 and A3.
- Black A2/B2 also had only A1 and A3.

I wrongly called this a shared-liberty position that neither player could start. Immediate capture reading was insufficient: Black can start because the White capture leaves a killable three-point eye space.

The actual continuation was:
43 B A3, 44 W A1 captured Black A2/A3/B2,
45 B A2 occupied the vital dividing point,
46 W G2, 47 B A3,
48 W G3, 49 B B2 captured all nine White lower-left stones.

Immediately after move 44, the empty eye space was A2/A3/B2. White A2 would divide it into two true eyes at A3 and B2, but it was Black's turn. Black A2 took that point first. After move 45:
- White's nine-stone group had A3 and B2 as its only liberties.
- Black A2 had the same two liberties.
- White A3 would leave both groups with only B2; Black B2 captures all ten White stones.
- White B2 similarly allows Black A3 to capture all ten.
- If White plays elsewhere, Black can fill one remaining liberty and then capture at the other, as happened.

Black A1 first in the earlier move-19 position also works by the same principle: White A3 captures A1/A2/B2, but Black A2 then occupies the vital point of the remaining A1/A2/B2 eye space. This is not an unconditional seki.

The eight-stone group did not become safe merely because both sides shared two liberties, and capturing three invading stones did not establish life. The opponent's next turn mattered. This explicitly corrects the claim made during play.

No single earlier replacement is established. Reconsider the left group's base before the B2 invasion and avoid treating the C2/B4/A4/C1 boundary sequence as a demonstrated living pattern. The observed outcome does not prove C3 or G7 wrong individually.

## A self-atari on the upper-left boundary
38 W B6, 39 B B7 left White B6 with only A6.
White A6 would extend to two stones with only A7; Black A7 would capture both and join B7.
40 W B8 instead secured the upper wall, and 41 B A6 captured B6.

The inventory caught the atari, but B6 had been played without checking the B7 cut and the extension's destination. This is a concrete one-stone loss, not proof that B6 has no possible strategic use. It gained no lasting living connection in this continuation.

## Lower-right invasion: one real eye, an unsecured second boundary
46 W G2, 48 W G3, 50 W F3,
51 B H3, 52 W H2, 53 B H4,
54 W J2, 55 B J3, 56 W H1.

H1 and J2 established a true corner eye at J1. A proposed second eye at G1 required a surviving White boundary at F1, which had not been secured. The next sequence was:
57 B F2, 58 W E2, 59 B F1,
60 W E3, 61 B E1.

F2/F1/E1 joined Black's D1–D4 chain. The attempted pressure at E2 did not capture the undercutting stones. G1 bordered Black F1 and therefore was not a White eye.

After move 61 the eight-stone White group E2/E3/F3/G2/G3/H1/H2/J2 had E4, F4, G1, G4 and J1 as liberties. Its remaining central strip was closed above by Black E5/F5/G5 and on the sides by D4/H4. E4/F4/G4 were raw liberties, not access to a new open region.

67 B G1, 69 B E4, 71 B F4 and 77 B G4 removed those liberties.
After move 77 the group had only J1. White J1 would be suicide because no surrounding Black group would be captured.
79 B J1 captured all eight stones.

This repeats games 2 and 4: preserving H1 and one corner eye was useful, but did not establish a second eye or a viable escape. Reassess immediately when F2 undercuts the F1 boundary. No saving alternative at move 58 was verified.

## What survived, and why
The upper framework connected through D8/E8/F8/F7/G7/G6, then H6/H7/J7. It ultimately scored only 25 area, insufficient by itself: 25 + 7 against 56.

The final life proof was explicit:
- 64 W D9, 65 B B9, 66 W C9 put B9 in atari with only A9.
- 68 W A9 captured B9 and made a true eye there, bordered by White A9/B8/C9.
- 70 W F9 made a separate true eye at E9, bordered by White D9/E8/F9.
All of those boundary stones belonged to the same connected upper group.

72 W pass was followed by 73 B H8, 74 W G8,
75 B H9, 76 W G9, 78 W J8,
80 W J9 captured H8/H9.
Before the last capture Black H8/H9 had only J9; White already had B9 and E9 and could fill J9 safely. This contrasts with the failed lower-left capture: the surviving group already had two independent eyes.

81 B pass, 82 W pass finished the game. Passing accepted a losing count and produced a verifiable score.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k. Practise a repeatable living base and a scored win before increasing rank.
2. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. Manually read the first fill, the capture, and the opponent's next attack on the resulting eye shape.
3. A three-point eye space requires its dividing point. If the opponent can occupy that point immediately after your capture, the capture may not save the group.
4. For an eye, name every boundary and verify that it connects and survives. J1 was real; G1 failed because F1 became Black. B9/E9 worked because every boundary was connected White.
5. Before a contact move, check the opponent's cut and the extension after atari. B6–A6 reached only A7 and did not escape.
6. Let the area count change the opening before the board closes. The surviving upper region scored 25; two additional failed groups contributed no final area. Do not count those bases as secure.
7. An earlier alternative opening/base plan remains a hypothesis. This game demonstrates specific failed continuations and life-reading errors, not optimal moves or a proven cause at a single opening point.

All choices and tactical reading were manual. Code only inspected present-board groups/liberties, recorded responses, converted the move record to SGF and counted final area. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move recommendations were used.

Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

## Record
- Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).
- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.
- Game 3: Black vs 8k, same rules. Lost by resignation after White move 64 (J5). Final captures: Black 1, White 2; no numerical final score.
- Game 4: White vs 12k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 43 (F1). Final captures: Black 1, White 0; no numerical final score.
- Game 5: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+12 after consecutive passes at moves 39–40. Area: Black 38, White 43 plus 7 komi. Final captures: 0 each; dead Black D8/D9/E8/E9 were removed for scoring.
- Game 6: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+24 after consecutive passes at moves 81–82. Area: Black 56, White 25 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 18, White 6; the nine-stone lower-left and eight-stone lower-right White groups were captured.
- Game 7: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+26 after consecutive passes at moves 61–62. Area: Black 31, White 50 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 1, White 4; Black F9/G9/H9 and the invading G2 stone were captured.
- Game 8: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+8 after consecutive passes at moves 75–76. Area: Black 48, White 33 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 11, White 4; the eight-stone lower-left and three-stone right White groups were captured. The top group lived and repelled two invasions.
- Game 9: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+42 after consecutive passes at moves 67–68. Area: Black 23, White 58 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 4, White 16; White captured fifteen left-side stones after winning the A1 ko for life. The right group lived with three independent two-point eye spaces.

- Read game-004.md for the fourth review; game-004.sgf and game-004-log.json contain all 43 moves and returned positions.
- Read game-005.md for the fifth review; game-005.sgf and game-005-log.json contain all 40 moves (37 stone moves, three passes) and returned positions.

1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. 8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.
27. Three corner approaches are not three living bases. In game 8, White C7/C3/G7/E7 built a surviving top wall, but C3 was left alone until move 22. After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
29. An edge strip also needs an outside boundary. Game 8's H3/H2/H1 had only J3/J2/J1 after Black H4/G2/G1. J4 was unsecured, so these were not two eyes. Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide because Black J2/J3 retained J4. Do not reuse this late entry as a living pattern.
30. Game 8's top main group had true eyes D7 (C7/D6/E7/D8) and E9 (D9/E8/F9), all boundaries connected White. B7/C8/C9 then contained A7/B8; A8 and B9 captured them. H8/G9/J9 captured H9. Rebuilding liberties after captures preserved the top, but its 33 area still lost to 48 plus the komi adjustment. Life and sufficient area remain separate tests.

31. Game 9's capture of White A4/A5 at move 45 left Black only A4/A5: one two-point eye. Black A1 later captured A2, but A1 itself had only A2. After B A5 captured the invading A4 stone, W A2 captured A1 and created a ko at A1; the fifteen-stone main group had only A4. No adequate forcing ko threat was established. B H5 connected the right side, but W A4 ignored it and captured fifteen. Captures and connected stones did not establish a second unconditional eye.
32. In game 9, White B1 undermined the left first-line eye boundary before the A4 invasion. B2/B3 and later B4/B5 did not fix it. Reconsider development before those undercuts and the vital eye-space invasion; no saving replacement is verified. The eleven-stone left group after move 35 had only an eighteen-point geometric outline, including unsecured A1/A2/A3/A4/A5/B4/B5, so saving that outline alone would not establish a winning total.
33. Game 9's right group lived after H5 connected its parts and H1/J3/J5 secured independent two-point eye spaces J1/J2 (H1/H2/J3 boundaries) and H4/J4 (G4/H3/H5/J3/J5 boundaries). J8 later secured a third space J6/J7 (H6/H7/J5/J8 boundaries). All boundaries were connected Black. Its 23 area still lost badly; H1 alone was not the life proof.

## Next-game focus
- Choose a rank deliberately. Games against 9d, 4k, 8k, 12k and 20k were lost. Keep 20k for another controlled experiment until living groups and scored wins are repeatable; no successful rank is established. 9d remains the target.
- Five games at 20k have now lost. Continue at 20k. Game 9 connected and preserved the right group but lost fifteen left stones in a ko for life and scored only 23 area. No successful opening or improved strength is established.
- As Black, address eye boundaries before an opponent's first-line undercut and vital-point invasion. In game 9, B2/B3 connection did not prevent White B1/A4 from undermining life. Reconsider left development around moves 29–35 before G8/H8; all replacements remain hypotheses. After every eye-space capture, name the new eyes and check isolated boundary stones for ko dependence.
- As White, reconsider lower-left development around move 10 before further top expansion. B3 or C2 then are unverified candidates; C2 alone does not establish life. Name both eye boundaries and the needed moves before counting the corner. Do not postpone a second viable base until the central wall closes.
- Keep opening alternatives as hypotheses. Securing a corner/lower-side position earlier (for example considering C3 before the upper-right exchanges) is worth trying, not established as best.
- Game 5 tried C3/G3/E5 and secured a surviving lower group but only 38 area. Reconsider the center/upper boundary earlier, for example move 11 before D6/F6 arrive; E6 then is an unverified candidate. Do not repeat the failed late E8 invasion continuation as a life pattern.
- Game 7 tried C3/G7/E5 with E6/E7/E8 and still had only a 38-point outline before the top loss. Earlier upper-boundary play alone did not solve the deficit. Count by rows/regions around moves 10–16 and contest additional space while invasion bases remain available; all opening replacements remain hypotheses.
- Before each move: identify atari/cuts, weakest group and eye prospects, largest area gain, and whether opponent can ignore the intended threat.
- In contact fights, inspect current-board groups/liberties before EVERY move. Game 4 did this and addressed the J4/J5 atari, but still lost the main group. Use the inventory to assess eye space and escape routes as well as immediate atari.
- Name eye boundaries and the required dividing move before calling a group safe. Preserve both corner boundaries and outside liberties; an invading stone's capture may still leave only one eye.
- Check whose turn it will be after a capture. A hypothetical dividing move does not prove life if the opponent gets to occupy that point first. Do not reuse game 6's lower-left sequence as a seki or living pattern.
- Count secure area and unsecured potential separately. Re-evaluate the base immediately after an undercut; do not defer it merely because the group has present liberties.
- Save complete move records, final result, and a small number of concrete lessons after each game. Update this file with the latest record and evidence.

const review=`# Game 10: White vs 20k — W+10

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 63–64. There were 64 moves: 61 stone moves and three passes (61, 63, 64).
Final captures: Black 0, White 4. No ko, invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first win in the series, following five losses at 20k. It establishes one successful game at 20k, not consistent strength or an optimal opening. Retain 20k until wins and living groups are repeatable, including as Black.

## Records and verified score
- game-010.sgf contains all 64 moves.
- game-010-log.json contains opponent selection, all 32 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty inventories, complete moves and independent area count.
- Official result: White wins by 10 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 26 stones + 13 territory = 39; White 31 stones + 11 territory = 42. White plus komi = 49. All 81 points are assigned; no neutral points.
- White's lower group: 14 stones plus E1/D2/D3 = 17 area.
- White's upper group: 17 stones plus A9/C8/D9/E9/F9/G9/H9/J9 = 25 area.
- Upper area by rows: all nine points in row 9, all nine in row 8, B7/C7/D7/E7/G7 (five), and C6/D6 (two): 25.
- Black territory: A5 and H1/J1/H2/J2/H3/J3/H4/J4/G5/H5/J5/J6.
- Black captured no White stones. The four captured Black stones were E1 at move 24 and C2/D2/D3 at move 26.

## Lower fight: cut, pressure the shared escape, then secure the eyes
Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4, 5 B C5,
6 W D4, 7 B D5, 8 W E3, 9 B D2,
10 W E4, 11 B F4, 12 W F3, 13 B G4.

E3 put D3 in atari, and Black D2 extended downward. E4 joined E3 to C3/C4/D4; F3 extended into still-open lower-right space. Unlike the late E4 extension in game 8, this extension had more than one temporary destination.

14 W C7 established an upper foothold while the lower group still had options.
15 B B4, 16 W B3, 17 B C2, 18 W B2,
19 B B1, 20 W E2, 21 B E1.

B3/B2 answered the left-side pressure, but B1 undercut the first-line boundary. The group was not yet alive. After move 21, Black C2/D2/D3 had only C1/D1; Black E1 had D1/F1.

22 W F1 reduced E1 to D1. Black ignored this atari with 23 B A4.
24 W D1 captured E1 and put C2/D2/D3 in atari at C1.
Black ignored that atari with 25 B A3.
26 W C1 captured C2/D2/D3.
27 B A2 kept Black B1 in atari at A1 while connecting the left-edge Black stones.

F1 before D1 mattered. In the actual move-21 position, immediate W D1 would be a self-atari at C1; B C1 captures that stone and opens D1 for the Black group. After F1, W D1 instead captures E1, opening E1 as a second liberty for the new White stone.

This limited reading is not a proof of every alternative or a forced win.

The capture at C1 did not itself prove life. White C1/D1 and F1 were still separate from the main group, and the empty C2/D2/D3 region was connected.
28 W F2 connected F1 to E2/F3.
29 B B5, 30 W C2 connected C1/D1 through B2/C3 and closed the left boundary of D2/D3.

After move 30 the lower group had two independent secured eye spaces:
- E1: bounded by White D1/E2/F1, all connected.
- D2/D3: bounded by White D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4, all connected.
This life proof held when Black G3/G2/G1 closed the remaining outside liberties. The final lower group had exactly E1/D2/D3 as liberties and was alive.

White did not chase the atari Black B1 by W A1 after move 27. That would capture B1 but leave the new isolated A1 stone with only B1, introducing a simple-ko dependency. F2/C2 secured unconditional eyes elsewhere instead.

## Upper development: make the second base large enough and repair each connection
31 B G3, 32 W E7, 33 B G2, 34 W G7, 35 B G1.
The lower group stayed alive but shrank to 17 area. The earlier C7 foothold allowed White to develop the open upper side, rather than attempting another late lower-right invasion.

36 W C6, 37 B F5, 38 W D6, 39 B B6,
40 W B7, 41 B A7, 42 W A8, 43 B A6,
44 W B8, 45 B E6, 46 W D7.

B8 immediately joined A8 to B7. A8 had only B8/A9 after Black A6; leaving it disconnected would have allowed further pressure. D7 then joined the left upper chain to E7.

47 B F7 cut between E7 and G7, with only F6/F8.
48 W F8 put it in atari; 49 B F6 connected it to Black's main group.
50 W E8 connected F8 to the left upper chain.
51 B G6 left White G7 only H7/G8.
52 W G8 joined G7 to F8 before 53 B H7 removed H7.
54 W H8, 55 B H6, 56 W J8 closed the upper-right boundary.
57 B A1 connected Black B1 to the main group.
58 W D8, 59 B J7.

The choice of F8 rather than F6 at move 48 avoided a counter-atari trap: W F6 would have only G6, and B G6 could capture it, reopening F6 for Black F7. The actual F8 had E8/G8/F9 and supplied a viable connection.

## Settle the eyes before accepting the winning count
60 W B9, 61 B pass, 62 W C9, 63 B pass, 64 W pass.

B9 first connected to B8 and made a true eye at A9, bounded by A8/B9.
C9 then connected through B9 and made a second true eye at C8, bounded by B8/C7/D8/C9.
All boundaries belong to the connected upper group. D9–J9 remained a third, larger eye space.

C9 would not have connected directly to B8 or D8: those are diagonal neighbors. The actual B9–C9 sequence supplied the stone connection needed for the life proof.

The formal row/region count came late, around moves 52–63: 17 lower plus 25 upper = 42, enough to beat Black's 39 with komi. Early area estimates were provisional and were not recorded as a detailed secure/potential count around moves 10–16. Improve that timing next game; this win does not erase the counting weakness.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k for repeatability, especially as Black. One win does not establish consistent strength.
2. A small living group can anchor a winning total if a second base is developed while open space remains. Here 17 lower + 25 upper won; no late right-side invasion was needed.
3. Use the capture's newly opened liberty explicitly. F1 before D1 meant D1 captured E1 and survived; immediate D1 would have been captured.
4. Finish connections and eye boundaries after a capture. F2/C2 established E1 and D2/D3; the capture alone did not.
5. Repair short-liberty stones before tenuki: A8–B8, F8–E8, and G7–G8 all survived. Check the new atari stone too: F6 would have failed to G6.
6. Name actual orthogonal connections, not diagonals. B9 before C9 produced two independent true eyes A9/C8.
7. Count by rows earlier. Preserve the separation between secure area and unsecured outlines even when the opponent plays weakly.

All moves and tactical variations were chosen/read manually. Code only parsed returned current boards, counted present groups/liberties and empty regions, recorded responses, and converted the move record to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.
27. Three corner approaches are not three living bases. In game 8, White C7/C3/G7/E7 built a surviving top wall, but C3 was left alone until move 22. After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
29. An edge strip also needs an outside boundary. Game 8's H3/H2/H1 had only J3/J2/J1 after Black H4/G2/G1. J4 was unsecured, so these were not two eyes. Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide because Black J2/J3 retained J4. Do not reuse this late entry as a living pattern.
30. Game 8's top main group had true eyes D7 (C7/D6/E7/D8) and E9 (D9/E8/F9), all boundaries connected White. B7/C8/C9 then contained A7/B8; A8 and B9 captured them. H8/G9/J9 captured H9. Rebuilding liberties after captures preserved the top, but its 33 area still lost to 48 plus the komi adjustment. Life and sufficient area remain separate tests.

31. Game 9's capture of White A4/A5 at move 45 left Black only A4/A5: one two-point eye. Black A1 later captured A2, but A1 itself had only A2. After B A5 captured the invading A4 stone, W A2 captured A1 and created a ko at A1; the fifteen-stone main group had only A4. No adequate forcing ko threat was established. B H5 connected the right side, but W A4 ignored it and captured fifteen. Captures and connected stones did not establish a second unconditional eye.
32. In game 9, White B1 undermined the left first-line eye boundary before the A4 invasion. B2/B3 and later B4/B5 did not fix it. Reconsider development before those undercuts and the vital eye-space invasion; no saving replacement is verified. The eleven-stone left group after move 35 had only an eighteen-point geometric outline, including unsecured A1/A2/A3/A4/A5/B4/B5, so saving that outline alone would not establish a winning total.
33. Game 9's right group lived after H5 connected its parts and H1/J3/J5 secured independent two-point eye spaces J1/J2 (H1/H2/J3 boundaries) and H4/J4 (G4/H3/H5/J3/J5 boundaries). J8 later secured a third space J6/J7 (H6/H7/J5/J8 boundaries). All boundaries were connected Black. Its 23 area still lost badly; H1 alone was not the life proof.

34. Game 10 won as White with two living groups: lower 17 area plus upper 25 = 42, against Black 39 plus White's 7 komi. A small living base can anchor a sufficient total if a second base develops before the board closes. C7 at move 14 supplied an upper foothold; after lower life at move 30, E7/G7/C6/D6 expanded the top. This is one successful continuation, not a proven optimal opening.
35. In game 10 after Black E1 at move 21, immediate White D1 would have only C1, and Black C1 could capture it and reopen D1. White F1 first put E1 in atari; Black ignored it. White D1 then captured E1 and gained E1 as a liberty, and C1 captured C2/D2/D3 after another ignored atari. The opened liberty changed the tactic. Black's mistakes do not establish a forced opening win.
36. Game 10's captures did not alone prove life. F2 connected isolated F1, then C2 joined C1/D1 to the main group. E1 (D1/E2/F1 boundaries) and D2/D3 (D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4 boundaries) were then independent true eye spaces, with every boundary connected White. Capturing B1 by A1 after move 27 would instead have introduced a ko through isolated A1; unconditional life was secured elsewhere.
37. Game 10 repaired short-liberty stones promptly: A8–B8, F8–E8, G7–G8. After Black F7 at move 47, White F6 would have had only G6; Black G6 could capture it and reopen F6. Actual White F8 had E8/G8/F9, put F7 in atari, and connected through E8 after Black F6. Check the new atari stone's own liberties.
38. Game 10's upper eyes were A9 (A8/B9 boundaries) and C8 (B8/C7/D8/C9 boundaries). B9 connected to B8 before C9 joined through B9; C9 is only diagonal to B8/D8. Do not mistake a diagonal boundary arrangement for a connected life proof. The final count was verified, but the detailed row count came late; count earlier around moves 10–16 next game.

## Next-game focus
- Choose a rank deliberately. Retain 20k until living groups and scored wins are repeatable. Game 10 is the first win, after five losses at 20k; consistent strength is not established. 9d remains the target.
- Continue at 20k, especially to establish a scored win as Black. Game 10 preserved every White stone and scored W+10; the lower capture depended on ignored ataris. Preserve the demonstrated reading and connection habits without treating the full opening as forced or best.
- As Black, address eye boundaries before an opponent's first-line undercut and vital-point invasion. In game 9, B2/B3 connection did not prevent White B1/A4 from undermining life. Reconsider left development around moves 29–35 before G8/H8; all replacements remain hypotheses. After every eye-space capture, name the new eyes and check isolated boundary stones for ko dependence.
- As White, reconsider lower-left development around move 10 before further top expansion. B3 or C2 then are unverified candidates; C2 alone does not establish life. Name both eye boundaries and the needed moves before counting the corner. Do not postpone a second viable base until the central wall closes.
- Game 10 offers a concrete White example: C3/C4/D4/E3/E4/F3 cut off Black D3 and kept lower-right access; B3/B2/E2 addressed undercuts; F1/D1/C1 captured, then F2/C2 secured two eyes. C7 was already present when E7/G7 expanded the upper base. Re-read its exact board and Black replies; do not transplant this sequence into game 8 or assume different replies fail.
- Keep opening alternatives as hypotheses. Securing a corner/lower-side position earlier (for example considering C3 before the upper-right exchanges) is worth trying, not established as best.
- Game 5 tried C3/G3/E5 and secured a surviving lower group but only 38 area. Reconsider the center/upper boundary earlier, for example move 11 before D6/F6 arrive; E6 then is an unverified candidate. Do not repeat the failed late E8 invasion continuation as a life pattern.
- Game 7 tried C3/G7/E5 with E6/E7/E8 and still had only a 38-point outline before the top loss. Earlier upper-boundary play alone did not solve the deficit. Count by rows/regions around moves 10–16 and contest additional space while invasion bases remain available; all opening replacements remain hypotheses.
- Before each move: identify atari/cuts, weakest group and eye prospects, largest area gain, and whether opponent can ignore the intended threat.
- In contact fights, inspect current-board groups/liberties before EVERY move. Game 4 did this and addressed the J4/J5 atari, but still lost the main group. Use the inventory to assess eye space and escape routes as well as immediate atari.
- Name eye boundaries and the required dividing move before calling a group safe. Preserve both corner boundaries and outside liberties; an invading stone's capture may still leave only one eye.
- Check whose turn it will be after a capture. A hypothetical dividing move does not prove life if the opponent gets to occupy that point first. Do not reuse game 6's lower-left sequence as a seki or living pattern.
- Count secure area and unsecured potential separately. Re-evaluate the base immediately after an undercut; do not defer it merely because the group has present liberties.
- Save complete move records, final result, and a small number of concrete lessons after each game. Update this file with the latest record and evidence.

## User constraints
Play each game to completion (passes or resignation allowed). Choose opponent before the first move.
Code may inspect the current board, count stones/liberties, check legality, and keep records. Do not build/use an engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or a program that selects/ranks/recommends moves.
